name: Proxima Centauri
kind: Nearest star to the Sun: a small red dwarf 4.2 light-years away

items.reason: The 2010 end sits on a Gaia star that does not move. The dot is that star, seen in one image and missed in the other.

changes.method: Dots seen only in WISE 2010 are paired with dots seen only in SPHEREx at 4.6 µm, 8″ to 190″ apart and of similar brightness. Each pair is then checked against the target's path, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD.
changes.not_checked: Asteroids and comets are not checked. An unconfirmed pair is not a discovery.

evidence.classification: Nearby star with fast proper motion

checks.text: Measured speed matches the catalogue: 3.82 vs 3.86″/yr (difference 1.1%)
Nearest Gaia DR3 star is 3.6″ from the typed position, so it may not be the object you meant. Very cold or fast objects (like WISE 0855 and Luhman 16) are often missing from Gaia.
Steady brightness between Jul 2025 and Feb 2026 (-0.06 ± 0.06 mag)
60 of 60 SPHEREx measurements flagged (overflow or bloom: the object is too bright for SPHEREx). No reliable SPHEREx spectrum, so we do not show one.

facts.headline: About 24 km/s across the sky
facts.detail: That is 0.8 times the speed of Earth around the Sun. It is sideways speed only: motion toward or away from us does not show in images.

facts.headline: Crosses the width of the full Moon in about 470 years
facts.detail: A typical star in these images needs more than 100,000 years, which is why this one stands out in a flipbook.

facts.headline: 4.2 light-years away: one of the Sun's nearest neighbours
facts.detail: The light in these images left it about 4.2 years ago.

facts.headline: About 2,800 K at its surface
facts.detail: That is 49% of the Sun's surface temperature (5,772 K), so it glows mostly in infrared light.
facts.basis: Gaia DR3 estimate from its colours

limits: Motion: an object must shift 2 SPHEREx pixels (12″) to count as moving. Over these 15.6 years that means faster than 0.79″ per year. Slower objects read as “no measurable motion”.
SPHEREx alone covers only 7 months here: by the same 2-pixel rule, enough only for motion faster than 22″ per year. The 2010 WISE image is what makes slower motion visible.
Brightness: compared at 2 SPHEREx visits only. A change between or outside those dates is not seen.
Bright stars: this one overflows SPHEREx pixels, so its spectrum and exact brightness are not reliable here.
Solar System: the page checks against Gaia stars only. It does not check asteroids or comets, so a moving dot without a Gaia circle may be a known asteroid.
Crowding: one SPHEREx pixel is 6.15″ wide, so two close objects can blend into one dot and one spectrum.
